catalog_quote: Stress (Accent). § 12. In all uncompounded words the chief stress falls upon the stem-syllable and always remains there even when suffixes and inflexional endings follow it. This syllable is always the first of the word. In compound words the chief stress falls upon the stem-syllable of the first component part if the second part is a noun or an adjective; and on the stem-syllable of the second part if this is a verb or derived from a verb. audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: both the Wright 1906 sec. 12 deciding quotation (p. 7) and the Braune 1891 secs. 9/55/75 corroborating quotations are verbatim in the held archive.org scanned files at the stated places. (2) Deciding source: a 1906 pedagogical primer backed by the 1891 edition of the standard reference grammar (Braune). For a dead corpus language there is no instrumental literature; the best current description is Braune/Heidermanns 17th ed. 2023 (not yet obtained, paywalled; verified via CrossRef). Glottolog lists only Wright as a grammar. publisher pages (De Gruyter, DNB) were bot-blocked. (3) downloaded the open-access Fulk 2018 comparative grammar; its sec. 2.2 confirms the classification exactly: fixed initial (root) stress, verbal prefixes unstressed

sources.citation: Fulk, R. D. 2018. A Comparative Grammar of the Early Germanic Languages (Studies in Germanic Linguistics 3). Amsterdam: John Benjamins. Open access, DOI 10.1075/sigl.3.
sources.quote: 'When the accent shifted in Proto-Germanic, in most lexical categories it came to rest on the initial syllable of the word ... The prefix *ga-/*gi- is never stressed, but other prefixes on nouns and adjectives were usually stressed ... The chief exception to the rule of initial stress is that verb roots receive primary stress, leaving prefixes unstressed or with a lesser degree of stress. The chief evidence for root-stress in verbs is of two kinds: alliterative patterns in verse and vowel reductions in prefixes.' n. 5: 'variation in the spelling of the OHG equivalent (fur-, for-, fir-, fer-) c

sources.note: A complete survey of acute/circumflex accent marks in OHG and OS manuscripts (four usage types, Notker's system as the consistent one). Conclusion p. 123: the accents are 'Tonzeichen' = marks of word accent (Betonung, i.e. stress, on the stem syllable, as in Latin grammatical practice), only secondarily quantity marks (Type I: circumflex on long, acute on short stressed vowels). 'Ton/Hochton' here is the philological term for stress; no pitch/tonal contrast is posited. tone.quote: Die Frage nach der Bedeutung der Accente im Althochdeutschen und Altsächsischen wird am richtigsten beantwortet werden: sie sind Tonzeichen (wie im Lateinischen), meist auf Stammsilben gesetzt, erst sekundär sind sie auch Zeichen der Quantität, die in ihren Funktionen manchmal noch zu trennen (Typus I: Circumflex auf Länge, Acut auf Kürze), meist aber nicht mehr reinlich zu scheiden sind (Typus II. III. IV). ... [p. 122] wenn der Circumflex im Deutschen, abweichend vom Lateinischen, auch auf die antepaenultima und noch weiter nach vorn gerückt werden konnte, also der Tonsilbe zustrebte, die in der Regel die Stammsilbe war.
tone.locator: p. 123 (and p. 122), 'Ergebnisse' following the survey of accent material; Betonung results pp. 128-132
tone.translation: The question of the meaning of the accents in Old High German and Old Saxon is best answered thus: they are accent marks [signs of the (stress) accent] (as in Latin), mostly placed on stem syllables; only secondarily are they also signs of quantity, functions that can sometimes still be separated (Type I: circumflex on a long, acute on a short vowel) but mostly can no longer be cleanly distinguished (Types II, III, IV). ... since the circumflex in German, unlike Latin, could be moved onto the antepenult and further forward, i.e. it gravitated to the accented syllable, which as a rule was the stem syllable.
tone.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone.summary: Accent marks = stress (stem/initial syllable) + vowel quantity; no tonal contrast described.

tone.quote: 2. Aber woher der Anfangsakzent? (Vgl. Scherer S. 80 ff.) Der grammatische Wechsel setzt die Verschiebung der idg. Tenues, also zugleich exspiratorischen und idg.-freien Akzent voraus. Das ergibt eine Übergangs-Periode, in der der idg. durch den sekundären exspiratorischen Anfangsakzent erdrückt, eine vorwiegend musikalische von einer vorwiegend exspiratorischen Betonung abgelöst wird, wie das z. B. am Italischen, Keltischen und später am Griechischen zu beobachten ist ... [§ 55] so ist es der exspiratorische Charakter des Akzents, der hier wirksam ist, d. h. auch die hochdeutsche Tenuisverschiebung ist noch eine Folge der germanischen Festlegung des Anfangsakzentes
tone.locator: sec. 153 'Schluß', p. 253; sec. 55 'Die Tenuisverschiebung', p. 92-93; sec. 6 'Akzent', p. 17
tone.translation: 2. But where does the initial accent come from? (Cf. Scherer p. 80 ff.) Verner alternation presupposes the shift of the IE tenues, hence an accent that was already expiratory and still IE-free. This yields a transitional period in which -- the IE accent being crushed by the secondary expiratory initial accent -- a predominantly musical accentuation is replaced by a predominantly expiratory one, as can be observed e.g. in Italic, Celtic and later in Greek ... [sec. 55] it is the expiratory character of the accent that is at work here, i.e. the High German tenues shift too is still a consequence of the Germanic fixing of the initial accent.
tone.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone.summary: Expiratory (dynamic) word-initial stress accent; IE musical accent replaced; no tone.
